item.title: One whose mind is like a rock, Firm, not shaken, Without greed for the agreeable, Without hatred for the disagreeable — One whose mind is…
item.description:
One whose mind is like a rock,
Firm, not shaken,
Without greed for the agreeable,
Without hatred for the disagreeable —
One whose mind is thus developed —
From where can suffering come?

From: Udana 4.4

item.title: Elder Telakāni: I sank deep in a lake, Full of mud, unable to escape — Full of deceit, envy, Tension and darkness. Thunder of restlessness…
item.description:
Elder Telakāni:

I sank deep in a lake,
Full of mud, unable to escape —
Full of deceit, envy,
Tension and darkness.

Thunder of restlessness resounded,
Clouds of fetters covered,
Waterfall of wrong thoughts,
Connected with sensual desire —
They swept me away
Into the ocean of wrong views.

Everywhere, streams flow,
Creepers stand and sprout.
Who can block those streams?
Who can cut down the creepers?

Venerable sir, make a dam,
Block those streams.
Do not let the water
Born of mind sweep you away,
As a rapid current sweeps away a tree.

So I, afraid,
Seeking the far shore from this shore,
Then the Teacher,
Attended by the noble Saṅgha,
With the weapon of wisdom,
Waits as a support for people.

He brought me, while sinking,
A well-made ladder —
The Buddha, pure, firm,
Made of the heartwood of Dhamma —
Then he said to me:
“Do not be afraid!”

Climbing the tower of mindfulness,
From there I contemplate
People who delight in identity view —
Formerly, I was proud.

When I saw the path,
The boat I needed to board,
I did not abide in a self,
Seeing the supreme destination.

The dart that arises from self,
Born from the cause of existence —
He taught the supreme path,
The cessation of those things.

The knot that for a long time,
Hidden, lay within the skin —
The Buddha untied and threw it away,
Removing all that is harmful.

From: Theragāthā 16.3

item.title: “Monk, when a person dwells with sense faculties guarded, with moderation in eating, committed to wakefulness, watching over wholesome states, devoted to developing the factors…
item.description:
“Monk, when a person dwells with sense faculties guarded, with moderation in eating, committed to wakefulness, watching over wholesome states, devoted to developing the factors of enlightenment at the beginning and end of the night — then his body does not feel intoxicated, his eye sees directions clearly, the Dhamma is remembered by him. Sloth and torpor do not overcome his mind. With gladness, he lives the holy life. He has no doubts about wholesome states. Therefore, monks, you should train thus: ‘I will guard the sense faculties … be devoted to developing the factors of enlightenment at the beginning and end of the night.’”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.56
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Having seen with wisdom, the defilements are abandoned. Monks, that monk is called one who has blinded Māra, destroyed his track, escaped the sight of…
item.description:
“Having seen with wisdom, the defilements are abandoned. Monks, that monk is called one who has blinded Māra, destroyed his track, escaped the sight of Māra. He has crossed beyond all clinging in the world. He walks confidently, stands confidently, sits confidently, lies down confidently. Why is that? Because he has escaped the reach of Māra.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 26 – Ariyapariyesanāsutta

item.title: “I do not see any other thing, monks, through which unarisen unwholesome states arise and arisen wholesome states decline, as intimacy with unwholesome states and…
item.description:
“I do not see any other thing, monks, through which unarisen unwholesome states arise and arisen wholesome states decline, as intimacy with unwholesome states and non-intimacy with wholesome states. Through intimacy with unwholesome states and non-intimacy with wholesome states, monks, unarisen unwholesome states arise and arisen wholesome states decline.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.72
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: Elder Māluṅkyaputta: Not lusting after forms, Seeing a form, mindful, The mind not clinging to the feeling, Not getting stuck, not remaining — As one…
item.description:
Elder Māluṅkyaputta:

Not lusting after forms,
Seeing a form, mindful,
The mind not clinging to the feeling,
Not getting stuck, not remaining —

As one sees a form,
Thus one feels the feeling —
Abandoning, not accumulating,
Mindful, practicing thus —

Thus, not storing up suffering,
He is said to be close to Nibbāna.

Not lusting after sounds,
Hearing a sound, mindful,
The mind not clinging to the feeling,
Not getting stuck, not remaining —

As one hears a sound,
Thus one feels the feeling —
Abandoning, not accumulating,
Mindful, practicing thus —
Thus, not storing up suffering,
He is said to be close to Nibbāna.

Not lusting after odors,
Smelling an odor, mindful,
The mind not clinging to the feeling,
Not getting stuck, not remaining —

As one smells an odor,
Thus one feels the feeling —
Abandoning, not accumulating,
Mindful, practicing thus —
Thus, not storing up suffering,
He is said to be close to Nibbāna.

Not lusting after tastes,
Tasting a flavor, mindful,
The mind not clinging to the feeling,
Not getting stuck, not remaining —

As one tastes a flavor,
Thus one feels the feeling —
Abandoning, not accumulating,
Mindful, practicing thus —
Thus, not storing up suffering,
He is said to be close to Nibbāna.

Not lusting after touches,
Feeling a touch, mindful,
The mind not clinging to the feeling,
Not getting stuck, not remaining —

As one feels a touch,
Thus one feels the feeling —
Abandoning, not accumulating,
Mindful, practicing thus —
Thus, not storing up suffering,
He is said to be close to Nibbāna.

Not lusting after phenomena,
Cognizing a phenomenon, mindful,
The mind not clinging to the feeling,
Not getting stuck, not remaining —

As one cognizes a phenomenon,
Thus one feels the feeling —
Abandoning, not accumulating,
Mindful, practicing thus —
Thus, not storing up suffering,
He is said to be close to Nibbāna.

From: Theragāthā 16.5

item.title: “Monks, when craving arises, where does it arise? When it establishes itself, where does it establish itself? Whatever in the world is endearing and agreeable:…
item.description:
“Monks, when craving arises, where does it arise? When it establishes itself, where does it establish itself? Whatever in the world is endearing and agreeable: In the world, the eye is endearing and agreeable. There this craving arises; there it establishes itself. The ear … the nose … the tongue … the body … the mind is endearing and agreeable. There this craving arises; there it establishes itself.”

From: Dīgha Nikāya 22 – Mahāsatipaṭṭhānasutta

item.title: - What fetters the world? What leads the world? By abandoning what thing Are all fetters cut? - Delight fetters the world, Seeking leads the…
item.description:
- What fetters the world?
What leads the world?
By abandoning what thing
Are all fetters cut?
- Delight fetters the world,
Seeking leads the world,
By abandoning craving,
All fetters are cut.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.65
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “‘Ignorance, ignorance,’ venerable sir, is said. What, venerable sir, is ignorance? And to what extent is one called ignorant?” - “Here, monk, an untaught ordinary…
item.description:
“‘Ignorance, ignorance,’ venerable sir, is said. What, venerable sir, is ignorance? And to what extent is one called ignorant?” - “Here, monk, an untaught ordinary person does not know as it actually is: ‘Form is subject to origination’ as form is subject to origination; he does not know as it actually is: ‘Form is subject to cessation’ as form is subject to cessation; he does not know as it actually is: ‘Form is subject to origination and cessation’ as form is subject to origination and cessation. This, monk, is called ignorance. And to that extent one is called ignorant.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.126

item.title: - What gives birth to a person? What always runs about? What undergoes rebirth? What does a person fear? - Craving gives birth to a…
item.description:
- What gives birth to a person?
What always runs about?
What undergoes rebirth?
What does a person fear?
- Craving gives birth to a person,
The mind itself always runs about,
Beings undergo rebirth,
Suffering is what a person fears.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.55
